findings.diagnosis: The prompt permits cuts that leave a sentence‑initial single-word function fragment (a lone determiner / pronoun / subordinating word / auxiliary) as its own piece; those tiny leading fragments lack a noun or predicate and often become contradicted or uninterpretable when translated separately.
findings.evidence: ids: [en_us_1116, en_us_101, en_us_633, en_us_70, en_us_525, en_us_1029, en_us_827, en_us_455] — each policy kept an initial tiny function-word piece (a single determiner/pronoun/subordinator/auxiliary) that the target attaches to the following material.
findings.type_predicate: A sentence with a candidate cut that would isolate a single sentence‑initial function word (a one‑word determiner/pronoun/subordinator/auxiliary) as its own piece, with no lexical noun or main verb within that piece.

edit.text: Do not place a cut that leaves a single sentence‑initial function word by itself; attach such a function word to the following words so the piece contains a noun or main predicate.

findings.diagnosis: The prompt undervalues cohesion between prepositions/particles and their complements and allows cuts that leave a prepositional or particle precursor alone; separating a preposition/particle from its object or clause frequently breaks attachment and yields high contradiction risk.
findings.evidence: ids: [en_us_292, en_us_1062, en_us_850, en_us_1052, en_us_1050, en_us_360, en_us_1082] — in each case the policy left a preposition/particle or similar one‑word precursor isolated, while the target keeps it with its complement.
